definition: Planning Poker, also known as Scrum Poker, is a collaborative consensus-based agile estimation technique. The team uses numbered cards to compare the effort, complexity and uncertainty of user stories.
Secret voting prevents the first opinion from influencing everyone else. After the simultaneous reveal, differences become a focused conversation about risks, requirements and technical approaches.

howCards.title: Main goal
howCards.text: Create a shared estimate with input from the whole team without favoring the most influential opinion.

howCards.title: Collaborative process
howCards.text: Combine individual reflection, simultaneous reveal and discussion to build understanding before reaching consensus.

process: The Product Owner presents the story and its acceptance criteria.
The team clarifies questions, dependencies, risks and scope boundaries.
Each participant chooses a card without showing anyone else.
Everyone reveals their cards at the same time.
People with the most distant estimates explain their reasoning.
The team votes again until it reaches a useful consensus.

fibonacci.title: Growing uncertainty
fibonacci.text: The larger the story, the less precise an estimate can be. Wider intervals represent that uncertainty.

fibonacci.title: No false precision
fibonacci.text: The team avoids spending time debating tiny differences between nearby values.

fibonacci.title: A signal to split
fibonacci.text: Very high estimates suggest that the story may need to be split or clarified.

benefits: Reduces anchoring bias and the influence of dominant opinions.
Reveals risks, dependencies and different interpretations of a requirement.
Helps the team plan with a consistent relative reference.
Turns differences in votes into objective conversations.

steps.title: Prepare the session
steps.text: Select refined stories, bring together the people who will do the work and choose the card scale.

steps.title: Present the story
steps.text: Explain the goal, expected value and acceptance criteria without suggesting an estimate.

steps.title: Discuss the scope
steps.text: Clarify questions and identify integrations, testing, risks and relevant technical work.

steps.title: Vote privately
steps.text: Each participant chooses the card that best represents effort, complexity and uncertainty.

steps.title: Reveal simultaneously
steps.text: Show all votes together so that assessments remain independent.

steps.title: Discuss the differences
steps.text: Start with the extremes and look for information that part of the team may not have considered.

steps.title: Vote again
steps.text: Repeat after the discussion. If disagreement remains, clarify or split the story.

guide.cardsIntro: A common scale uses 0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13 and 21. The wider intervals reflect growing uncertainty.
specialCards: ? — there is not enough information to estimate
21+ — the story probably needs to be split
tips: Include the people who will implement and test the work.
Keep the conversation focused on the story scope.
Do not use story points to compare people or teams.
Record important assumptions discovered during the discussion.
Refine the scale based on the team's own context.

faq.question: Does Planning Poker estimate hours?
faq.answer: Teams usually use story points to compare effort, complexity and uncertainty. Hours can be used, but they may imply precision that does not exist yet.

faq.question: How many people should participate?
faq.answer: Include the people needed to perform and understand the work. Smaller groups make discussion easier; large teams can split the session.

faq.question: What if the team cannot agree?
faq.answer: Explore the extremes, clarify assumptions and vote again. If the difference remains, gather more information or split the story.

faq.question: Does it work for remote teams?
faq.answer: Yes. An online room preserves private choices, simultaneous reveal and equal participation across locations.

faq.question: What is Planning Poker?
faq.answer: Planning Poker is a consensus-based agile estimation technique in which team members privately choose numbered cards to estimate effort, complexity and uncertainty.

faq.question: How does Planning Poker work?
faq.answer: The Product Owner presents a story, the team discusses it, everyone chooses a card privately, and all cards are revealed together. Differences are discussed before another round.

faq.question: Why use the Fibonacci sequence?
faq.answer: The growing gaps in the Fibonacci sequence reflect the increasing uncertainty involved in estimating larger work items.

faq.question: What are the main benefits?
faq.answer: It reduces anchoring bias, includes every team member, exposes risks early and builds a shared understanding of the work.

faq.question: What is the difference between story points and hours?
faq.answer: Story points express relative effort, complexity and uncertainty. Hours are absolute time estimates and vary more between people and contexts.

faq.question: How many people should participate?
faq.answer: Three to nine estimators usually provides enough perspectives without making the discussion difficult to manage.

faq.question: How long should a session last?
faq.answer: Keep sessions focused, take regular breaks and avoid extending a single session beyond two or three hours.

faq.question: Which card values should we use?
faq.answer: Most teams use a modified Fibonacci deck together with special cards such as question mark, break and infinity.

faq.question: How do we run Planning Poker remotely?
faq.answer: Use a shared real-time room, establish clear facilitation rules and make sure every participant can discuss and vote independently.

faq.question: What should we do when there is no consensus?
faq.answer: Ask the highest and lowest estimators to explain their reasoning, discuss overlooked risks, and vote again. Split the story if uncertainty remains high.

faq.question: How should we handle very large stories?
faq.answer: Break large stories into smaller, independently valuable slices before trying to commit to an estimate.

faq.question: What is the Product Owner’s role?
faq.answer: The Product Owner explains the story, answers requirement questions and defines acceptance criteria without steering the technical estimate.

faq.question: How should the Scrum Master facilitate?
faq.answer: Keep the discussion focused, manage time, include every voice and remain neutral about the estimate itself.

faq.question: How do acceptance criteria affect estimation?
faq.answer: Clear acceptance criteria reduce ambiguity and help everyone estimate the same expected outcome.

faq.question: How do we identify dependencies?
faq.answer: Discuss external APIs, other teams, infrastructure and prerequisite work, then include their uncertainty in the conversation.

faq.question: How is team velocity calculated?
faq.answer: Add the story points completed in each sprint and use the average of several sprints for planning, never as an individual performance target.

faq.question: How do we include new team members?
faq.answer: Explain the scale and process, let them ask questions, and value their fresh perspective even while they learn the domain.

faq.question: Is Planning Poker the same as backlog refinement?
faq.answer: No. Refinement prepares and clarifies backlog items; Planning Poker is one estimation technique that can be used during refinement.

faq.question: Is group estimation better than individual estimation?
faq.answer: Group estimation combines perspectives and uncovers assumptions that an individual estimate is likely to miss.

faq.question: How should architecture be considered?
faq.answer: Discuss code complexity, technical debt, refactoring, non-functional requirements and architectural impact before voting.

faq.question: How can retrospectives improve estimates?
faq.answer: Review where estimates diverged from reality, identify missing assumptions and use those lessons in future refinement sessions.

faq.question: What should we look for in an online tool?
faq.answer: Prioritize ease of use, real-time synchronization, remote-team support, useful history and a workflow that does not distract the conversation.

faq.question: How can we measure success?
faq.answer: Look for better shared understanding, lower uncertainty, more predictable delivery and team satisfaction—not perfect numeric accuracy.

faq.question: How does Planning Poker affect team culture?
faq.answer: It promotes transparency, shared responsibility and open technical discussion while reducing blame around uncertain estimates.

faq.question: Does it work for large projects and multiple teams?
faq.answer: Yes. Estimate within each team and align scales and assumptions across teams without forcing every team to share identical velocity.
